question: m12
q: Is electricity inflation running ahead of overall inflation?

transcript.answer:
**Yes, by a wide margin.** In the year to **August 2026**, electricity prices rose **13.2%**. Overall inflation (the all-groups CPI) was **4.0%**, so electricity is rising more than three times as fast.

**How the gap has moved (year-on-year, Australia)**

| Period | Electricity | All groups |
|---|---|---|
| Jun 2025 | −6.3% | 1.9% |
| Oct 2025 | 37.1% | 3.8% |
| Feb 2026 | 37.0% | 3.7% |
| Jun 2026 | 22.4% | 3.8% |
| Jul 2026 | 6.1% | 3.5% |
| Aug 2026 | 13.2% | 4.0% |

**What this shows:**
- **It's been ahead for over a year.** Electricity has outpaced overall inflation every month from July 2025 onward. Before that, in the first half of 2025, electricity prices were *falling* year-on-year (between −5.9% and −13.2%).
- **The peak was in late 2025 and early 2026.** Annual electricity inflation was in the 20s and 30s, reaching 37.1% in October 2025 and 37.0% in February 2026.
- **The gap has narrowed recently.** It fell to 6.1% in July 2026, then rose again to 13.2% in August. That's still well above overall inflation, which has stayed between about 3.5% and 4.6% this year.

**A caveat on reading these numbers:** The CPI measures what households actually pay, so government power-bill rebates directly change it. The jump from negative to strongly positive in mid-2025, and the large month-to-month swings since, look like the effect of rebates being paid or wound back, not just changes in underlying power prices. That's my reading of the pattern; the data alone doesn't show the cause. So the 13.2% headline probably overstates how fast wholesale or retail tariffs are rising right now. Either way, households' electricity costs are rising much faster than prices overall.

*Source: ABS Monthly CPI, original series, annual % change, data to August 2026.*
